key_terms.meaning: Address generated by the CPU; the MMU translates it before memory is accessed.
Address seen by the memory unit and placed on the memory bus.
Hardware that maps logical addresses to physical addresses using base/limit registers or page tables.
Limit checks the logical address size; physical address = logical address + base after the check passes.
Copying an entire process between main memory and a backing store to free memory.
Each process occupies one continuous block of physical memory.
Free memory splits into small holes that cannot satisfy a request although total free space is enough.
Fixed-size block of a process's logical address space; size is a power of two.
Fixed-size block of physical memory; same size as a page.
Per-process table that maps page numbers to frame numbers.
Small fast associative cache of recent page-table entries.
Page table split into levels so unused regions need no leaf tables.
One table entry per physical frame, indexed by frame, storing the owning process and page.
Variable-length logical units such as code, stack and heap, each with a base and limit.
Loading a page into memory only when it is first referenced.
Trap raised when a referenced page is not present in memory.
Parent and child share pages read-only until one writes, then the written page is copied.
FIFO evicts the oldest page; LRU evicts the least recently used; optimal evicts the page used farthest in future.
Policy that decides how many physical frames each process receives.
A process spends more time paging than executing because it has too few frames.

takeaways: Logical addresses isolate processes; the MMU translates them only after a limit check.
Swapping frees memory by moving whole processes to a backing store, but it is slow.
Contiguous allocation creates holes and external fragmentation; compaction is costly.
Paging removes external fragmentation but adds page-table lookup cost and some internal fragmentation on the last page.
The TLB caches recent translations and makes paging fast in practice.
Large address spaces need multi-level, hashed or inverted page tables to avoid huge flat tables.
Segmentation matches the programmer's view of code, stack and heap but requires base and limit checks.
Demand paging loads pages lazily, so a process can start fast and be larger than physical memory.
Replacement algorithms choose victim pages; LRU approximates optimal, while FIFO can show Belady's anomaly.
Too few frames cause thrashing; allocation and working-set policies must give each process enough frames.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress definitions, diagrams, address translation, replacement counts and thrashing fixes across contiguous allocation, paging, segmentation and virtual memory.

bank.q: Define logical and physical address. Explain with a diagram how an MMU uses base and limit registers to translate an address and trap illegal accesses.
outline: Logical address is CPU-generated; physical address is memory-unit address.
Limit register checks logical address < limit.
Physical address = logical address + base.
Illegal access traps to the OS.
Diagram shows CPU, MMU, base/limit registers and memory.

bank.q: Explain swapping. Why is a backing store needed, and what costs make swapping expensive?
outline: Swapping copies a whole process out and later back in.
Backing store is fast disk space for swapped images.
Cost includes disk transfer time and context switching.
Swapping whole processes is coarse compared with paging.
It allows more processes to take turns in limited memory.

bank.q: Compare contiguous allocation, paging and segmentation. State one fragmentation or overhead problem of each.
outline: Contiguous allocation needs one continuous block and causes external fragmentation.
Paging uses fixed pages and frames; it removes external fragmentation but adds page-table overhead.
Segmentation uses variable segments matching code, stack and heap.
Segmentation can cause external fragmentation.
Each scheme needs address translation and protection checks.

bank.q: Describe the structure of a page table for a 64-bit address space. Explain two-level paging and why flat tables are impractical.
outline: Flat table needs one entry per virtual page.
64-bit space makes flat tables far too large.
Two-level paging splits the page number into outer and inner indexes.
Unused regions need no leaf tables.
Extra memory accesses are reduced by the TLB.

bank.q: A system has 32-bit logical addresses and 4 KB pages. A two-level page table uses 10 bits for the outer index and 10 bits for the inner index. Compute page offset, number of entries per table and total virtual pages. Show steps.
outline: 4 KB = 2^12, so page offset is 12 bits.
Page number is 32 − 12 = 20 bits.
10 + 10 = 20 bits, so the split matches.
Entries per table = 2^10 = 1024.
Total virtual pages = 2^20.

bank.q: Given page reference string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2,1,2,0,1,7,0,1 and three frames, run FIFO, LRU and optimal. Count faults and identify Belady's anomaly if any.
outline: Simulate FIFO with a queue; evict the oldest page.
Simulate LRU by tracking last use; evict least recently used.
Simulate optimal by looking ahead; evict farthest future use.
Count faults for each algorithm.
Belady's anomaly occurs if more frames increase FIFO faults for a suitable string.

bank.q: A process has four segments: code base 1000 limit 400, data base 2000 limit 300, stack base 5000 limit 200, heap base 7000 limit 100. Translate logical addresses (code, 350), (data, 320), (stack, 100), (heap, 50); state which trap.
outline: Check offset < segment limit.
Data 320 > 300: trap.

bank.q: For a demand-paged system with effective access time EAT = (1−p) × 100 ns + p × 10 ms, find p for EAT ≤ 200 ns. Interpret the result.
outline: Convert 10 ms to 10,000,000 ns.
The page-fault rate must be below about one fault per 100,000 accesses.

bank.q: Evaluate FIFO, LRU and optimal page replacement. Why is optimal not implementable? How does LRU approximate it, and what is Belady's anomaly?
outline: FIFO is simple but ignores recent use.
LRU uses past recency as a prediction of future use.
Optimal uses future reference knowledge and is a benchmark.
Optimal is not implementable online.
Belady's anomaly is more faults with more frames, seen in FIFO.

bank.q: Analyze thrashing using the working-set model. How can the OS detect it, and what allocation policies prevent it?
outline: Thrashing means high paging activity and low CPU use.
Working set is the set of pages used in a recent window.
Sum of working sets must fit in available frames.
If not, suspend or reduce multiprogramming.
Allocate enough frames per process to hold its working set.

bank.q: A system spends 80% of time paging and 20% executing. Increasing multiprogramming raises page faults. Explain the feedback loop and propose three fixes.
outline: More processes compete for fewer frames.
Each process faults more and waits for disk.
CPU use falls and the OS may add more processes, worsening thrashing.
Fixes include reducing multiprogramming, better replacement and working-set allocation.
Local replacement and enough frames per process help.

bank.q: Compare copy-on-write fork with eager copying. Give memory and time trade-offs, and explain when copy-on-write is beneficial.
outline: Eager copy duplicates all pages immediately.
Copy-on-write shares pages read-only until a write.
COW saves memory and makes fork fast.
Writes cause page-fault copies later.
COW helps when the child calls exec or mostly reads.

bank.q: Design a memory manager for a phone with limited RAM: choose paging or segmentation, page size, replacement and frame allocation. Justify choices against fragmentation, TLB reach and thrashing.
outline: Paging is a strong base; segmentation may be combined for logical protection.
Page size trades TLB reach against internal fragmentation.
LRU-like or clock replacement suits locality.
Frame allocation must avoid thrashing under memory pressure.
Justify using fragmentation, TLB, working-set and power or latency costs.

glossary.def: The set of logical addresses a process may use.
Register holding the start physical address added to a logical address.
Register holding the size of a process's logical address space.
Hardware unit that translates logical addresses into physical addresses.
Moving a whole process between main memory and a backing store.
Disk area that holds swapped-out process images.
A free block of memory in a contiguous allocation scheme.
Free memory split into holes too small for a request.
Wasted space inside an allocated block larger than the request.
Moving allocated blocks to combine free memory into one large hole.
Fixed-size block of logical memory in a paging system.
Fixed-size block of physical memory in a paging system.
Per-process table mapping page numbers to frame numbers.
One entry in a page table holding a frame number and control bits.
Fast cache of recent page-table translations.
Page table organised in levels to avoid storing unused entries.
Table with one entry per physical frame rather than per virtual page.
Division of a program into variable-length logical segments.
Table storing base and limit for each segment of a process.
Technique that lets a process use more logical memory than physical memory.
Loading pages only when they are referenced.
Trap raised when a referenced page is not in memory.
Sharing pages until a write forces a private copy.
More page frames causing more faults under FIFO replacement.
Set of pages a process has used in a recent time window.
High paging activity that leaves little time for useful execution.
